title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI is used to generate personalized outreach emails at scale, mimicking a well-known public figure to deceive targets into paying money. The failure is not in a deployed AI product but in the weaponization of AI capabilities by external actors, who use the technology to lower the cost of crafting convincing, individualized messages that reference the target's specific work. The scam operates at the solicitation stage, before any interview or production process begins, and it succeeds because the messages are detailed enough to appear credible.

The tell-tale signs appear late in the exchange, when a payment request arrives, rather than at first contact. A recipient who verified the request through official channels before engaging further would likely catch it, but the initial emails are designed to seem legitimate enough that many targets may not think to check. WHYY, NPR, and Fresh Air have confirmed awareness of the scheme and have stated they do not charge guests, which provides a clear factual baseline against which any such request can be measured.

What is not established is the identity of the individuals running the scam, the total number of people targeted or deceived, or the precise AI tools used to generate the emails.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been sending personalized emails to authors, entertainers, and other public figures impersonating Terry Gross and claiming to offer interviews on the NPR show "Fresh Air." The fraudulent messages include detailed references to the target's work and appear to come from legitimate production staff. However, the scam eventually requests money for production costs, typically around $250. WHYY, NPR, and "Fresh Air" have confirmed they are aware of these fraudulent emails and stress that they never charge guests for interviews or pay people to appear on their programs.

Cybersecurity experts attribute the success of these scams to artificial intelligence, which allows criminals to create highly convincing, personalized impersonations cheaply and at scale. Red flags include requests for payment, emails from suspicious addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com," and unusually direct contact from famous hosts rather than production assistants. Experts recommend verifying any suspicious interview requests by contacting the organization directly through official channels rather than responding to the suspicious message.
